text: Why do your ears pop on a plane?
Behind each eardrum is a tiny pocket of air.
It connects to your throat through a thin tube.
On the ground, the pressure on both sides matches.
But as the plane climbs, the cabin air thins out.
The air behind your eardrum pushes outward.
So the tube pops open and lets it escape.
Landing is the opposite, and it is harder.
The outside air pushes in, and the tube stays shut.
So swallow, yawn, or chew to pull it open.
That click? Your ears just matched the sky.
Follow for the next tiny why.
